summary: We developed MarsPath, an interactive, multi-layered GIS and expedition planning platform for Mars's Jezero Crater. It integrates authentic NASA and USGS data—including MRO HiRISE imagery, MGS MOLA altimetry, and CRISM spectroscopy—with a custom physics and bioenergetics engine.   To address the challenge of planetary exploration, MarsPath transforms static orbital maps into actionable mission intelligence. It evaluates candidate traverse routes based on Martian gravity, terrain friction, and dust optical depth to calculate exact metabolic oxygen costs and travel times. We also built a context-aware AI Site Analyst that monitors live telemetry to prevent fatal life-support deficits, alongside an Augmented Reality (AR) Visor HUD for 3D terrain visualization.   MarsPath is important because it bridges the critical gap between raw planetary data and astronaut safety. By proving that the shortest geometric path is often not the safest due to terrain hazards and high friction, it empowers mission planners to maximize astrobiological science return while strictly preserving vital oxygen reserves.
details:
What it does and how it works MarsPath is an interactive, multi-layered Geographic Information System (GIS) and expedition planner tailored for Jezero Crater. It works by fusing authentic NASA orbital telemetry with a custom biomechanical physics engine. When users select mission waypoints and adjust environmental variables like dust optical depth ($\tau$), the engine evaluates multiple candidate traverse routes. It calculates exact metabolic oxygen ($\text{O}_2$) costs, travel durations, and radiation exposure by factoring in Martian gravity, localized MOLA elevation changes ($\Delta h$), and terrain friction ($\mu$) derived from USGS geologic units.

Benefits and intended impact The core benefit of MarsPath is preventing fatal life-support deficits. It mathematically proves that a longer traverse on a smooth basin floor is often much safer and more oxygen-efficient than a shorter path over high-friction boulder fields. The intended impact is to provide mission control and future astronauts with a reliable decision-support system that maximizes astrobiological science return while rigorously protecting the 85-liter emergency reserve of the Primary Life Support System (PLSS).

Creativity Our project approaches mission planning creatively by translating dense planetary datasets into an immersive, human-centric interface. We built a 3D-pitched Augmented Reality (AR) Helmet Visor HUD that overlays route corridors and elevation contours directly onto the user's field of view. Additionally, rather than acting as a generic chatbot, our AI Site Analyst operates as a context-aware flight surgeon—injecting live mission state data to generate structured field briefings and oxygen warnings. We also designed a Plain-English Cost Analyzer that converts complex physics into simple comparative insights.

Factors considered We prioritized scientific transparency by strictly separating direct NASA/USGS observations from geological interpretations. We also heavily considered environmental unpredictability; the platform features an automatic Emergency Abort protocol that triggers when dust storms reach critical opacity ($\tau \ge 2.2$), instantly plotting the shortest return vector to the main station. Finally, we ensured reliability by building a deterministic local offline physics engine that guarantees the application functions even if planetary communication links fail.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript.
  • Libraries & APIs: Leaflet.js for OGC equirectangular planetary mapping, and the Google Gemini 3 Flash API for the live AI Site Analyst.
  • NASA/USGS Data Sources: Mars Trek WMTS (MRO HiRISE and CTX mosaics), MGS MOLA Color Shaded Relief altimetry, USGS Planetary Geologic Maps, MRO CRISM spectral mineralogy, and Perseverance MEDA/RAD environmental baselines.
